meaning_fix: If she (or it) doesn't come, start without me
reasoning: إجت is the 3rd person feminine past, ijat, 'she/it came'. 'If I don't come' would be إذا ما إجيت (iza ma jiit). ذ is z in إذا (iza). The plural imperative of بلّش is ballshu, with the i dropped.
Standard adjective pattern af3al, amlas, used for smooth surfaces and skin. It can also cover slippery, though mzallig is the more usual word for slippery.
ط is emphatic, so a capital T. The vowels are long aa then short i. The plural is Talaba or Tullaab.
ث is t in urban Palestinian, and the diphthong aw becomes long oo, so toor rather than thawr.
Geminate verb with emphatic ض, written as doubled capital DD. It is the 3rd person masculine past, 'he bit'.
Long oo, as in Palestinian loon, not lawn. The plural is alwaan.

An MSA-origin word of place that Palestinians really use for a parking spot or stop. ق is a glottal stop in this everyday word. The vowel after the w is a, maw'af; I am less sure whether aw stays or becomes oo here.
Literally 'he put his hand in the fire', meaning he took a risk or got into a dangerous situation. bi + il-naar is said bin-naar. ط is emphatic, so TT.
Intensive pattern fa33aal with shadda on ش. Taa marbuta after ف is e. Used for a clothes dryer.
Palestinians use form II khabbar for 'to tell/inform', so 'I tell you (m.)' is akhabbrak, not MSA ukhbirak. kaan laazim is the normal 'should have'. a7kiilak is a common alternative.
Negative imperative with laa plus the subjunctive, 2nd person feminine tit3abi. The urban feminine 'your' suffix is -ik, so 7aalik.
ص is emphatic, so a capital S. Taa marbuta after an emphatic is a.
Literally 'on my head, from above'. It is a warm reply to a request, meaning gladly or at your service. In foo', ق is a glottal stop and the vowel is long oo.
Everyday word, so ق is a glottal stop. Taa marbuta after ر is a. The plural is maqaabir, which keeps [q].
Idiom 'he mounted his head', meaning he dug in his heels and insisted. The pronoun -o is 'his'.
yoom has a long oo. The article assimilates to س, so is-sabt. Palestinians also just say is-sabt.
In isolation it is said 7ayaa with a long final aa. The t appears only in construct, as in 7ayaat-ak.
lamma 'when' has a doubled m. Palestinian says zghiir for صغير, with ص voiced to z. kunt is 'I was'.

meaning_fix: I want it / him (with stress on the object); the plain way to say 'I want it' is biddo
reasoning: biddi plus iyyaah is grammatical and used for emphasis ('I want THAT one'). Ordinary 'I want it' attaches the pronoun to bidd-: biddo (m.), bidha (f.).
warja/warjiini for 'show' is Lebanese and northern usage. A Ramallah speaker says warra (warrini = show me).
MSA-origin word in normal use. The y is doubled, and taa marbuta after ي is e. The plural is aghaani.
bti'Sud is the b- present of 'to mean/intend' for 'you' (m.). ق is a glottal stop and ص is emphatic. The ellipsis is not romanized.
Form IV past, 'he insulted'. It is of MSA origin, but ahaanni and ihaane are genuinely used in conversation.
Long oo, as in Palestinian khoof. Said the same way in everyday speech.
The gloss 'israel (Palestine)' is confusing: the word means Israel, the state, and the parenthetical does not fit it. The pronunciation has long aa, a glottal stop and long ii.
